We all know sleep is important, but sleep tracking may have an unintended downside. 

Researchers told a group of adults they’d measured their REM sleep from the night before, then made up the numbers. 

Half were told they’d had great REM sleep, half were told theirs was below average — none of it was real. 

Those who were told they’d slept poorly actually performed worse the next day on tests of attention and processing speed, even though their real sleep was untouched. 

Your brain, it turns out, will happily sabotage you based on a number someone hands you. Which is worth remembering the next time your sleep tracker flashes a low score at 6am. 

There’s even a name for what happens when you start organizing your life around that number: orthosomnia, a real and growing anxiety disorder built entirely around chasing perfect sleep data. 

The take-home: sleep is crucial for so many reasons, but if you have a bad night here or there, it’s probably not the Doomsday scenario your sleep tracker is telling you it is.

Next time you’re invited to a dinner party, skip the wine. Bring a nice bottle of extra-virgin olive oil instead. Trust me—I now do this and people love it.

Wine gets opened and forgotten. Olive oil, on the other hand, stays on the table, in the kitchen, in your body—doing good things like dampening inflammation and improving vascular function (PMID: 26378571). And unlike drinking too much (we’ve all been there), olive oil doesn’t cloud your memory—it may help protect it.

In a prospective cohort study (PMID: 38709531) of 92,383 adults followed for 28 years, those who consumed more than 7 grams of olive oil per day had a 28% lower risk of dying from dementia-related causes compared to those who rarely or never consumed it. That’s correlation, not causation, but there is solid evidence to support a potential causal pathway which I’ve documented in my book Genius Foods. And that’s just one of many benefits linked to real extra-virgin olive oil.

Plus, a beautiful bottle of EVOO doubles as a design object. Leave it on the table as a centerpiece—it says “I care about your brain and your tablescape.”

Buying tips:
- Look for a harvest date (freshness matters)
- Go for dark glass bottles to preserve antioxidants
- Make sure it’s “extra-virgin” and God-forbid not a blend of other oils
- While it may seem like a flex to go for a big Costco-size bottle, olive oil is best fresh. The smaller the bottle, the less time the oil will be exposed to air, and the fresher it will keep. Go small!
- A little peppery burn or grassy bite? That means it’s legit.

Olive oil is health food, conversation starter, and dinner party power move all in one. So would you do this?

Dark showering is one of my favorite simple rituals I recommend to all of our telehealth patients who are struggling with nervous-system overload, poor sleep, or that constant “wired but tired” feeling. By turning off the lights and showering in complete (or near-complete) darkness, you shut down visual noise—the relentless stream of bright screens, overhead lights, and environmental stimuli that keeps your sympathetic nervous system on high alert all day. This rapid drop in visual input signals safety to your brain, quickly shifting you into parasympathetic rest-and-digest mode, lowering cortisol, and allowing melatonin production to begin earlier in the evening. 
 
To deepen the sensory reset, add a few drops of calming lavender, pine, ylang ylang or eucalyptus essential oil or a handful of fresh eucalyptus or lavender leaves right under the shower stream—the warm water releases their therapeutic compounds, creating an aromatherapy steam that further calms the nervous system while supporting respiratory and skin health. If total pitch black feels too intense at first, simply light one small candle on the counter; the soft flicker is still gentle enough to keep visual stimulation minimal.

☕ Your morning coffee may be doing more than helping you wake up.

A new study published in JAMA followed more than 131,000 people for up to 43 years and found that drinking 2–3 cups of caffeinated coffee per day was associated with an 18% lower risk of dementia compared with drinking little or none.

People with higher caffeinated coffee intake were also less likely to report subjective cognitive decline and performed modestly better on certain measures of cognitive function.

The strongest associations were seen with moderate coffee intake—about 2–3 cups per day.

Researchers believe coffee's benefits may come from more than just caffeine. Coffee is rich in bioactive compounds, including polyphenols, that may help reduce inflammation and oxidative stress—two processes that are closely linked to brain aging. 

This doesn't mean coffee prevents dementia or guarantees protection. This was an observational study, so it can't prove cause and effect. But it adds to growing evidence that the habits we practice consistently over decades can influence brain health as we age.

Your daily habits matter. Sleep. Exercise. Blood sugar control. A nutrient-dense diet. Strong social connections. And yes... your morning cup of coffee may be one small piece of the puzzle. ☕🧠

We've been telling women mammograms save lives for decades. They don't.

There's never been a clinical trial, not one, that shows mammogram screening lowers the number of women who die from breast cancer. The Swedish trial followed 600,000 women. The Canadian study followed 90,000. Same death rate whether they got screened or not.

Mammograms use ionizing radiation to build the image. That's not controversial, that's physics. We know x-rays cause cancer everywhere else in medicine. The tissue that needs more radiation to image, dense breast tissue, is exactly where more radiation raises the risk.

Meanwhile 80% of mammogram triggered biopsies come back benign.

My guest this week is Dr. Jenn Simmons. She was the first fellowship trained breast surgeon in Philadelphia and the first oncoplastic surgeon in Pennsylvania. She recommended mammograms to thousands of women for twenty years. Then she got her own diagnosis at 46, and everything she thought she knew came apart.

She walks me through why mammograms don't hold up, what DCIS overtreatment actually costs women, and the two alternatives she's built her whole practice around now: a five minute at home tears test and a radiation free imaging technology that reads more like an MRI than an x-ray.

In my telehealth clinic, I see women who were never told any of this before they signed the consent form.

Simple way to lose some body fat, if you’re a short sleeper. 

In this randomized trial, adults with overweight who were habitually sleep deprived (sleeping <6.5 hours/night) were coached to sleep about an hour longer. 

Without being told to diet or exercise, they spontaneously ate ~270 fewer calories per day on average and lost a small amount of weight.

This doesn’t mean sleeping an extra hour is a magic fat-loss hack—if you’re already getting enough sleep, you probably shouldn’t expect the same effect. 

But if you’re chronically cutting sleep short, improving it may be one of the easiest ways to make eating less feel effortless.

You could be 40 or 50 years away from knowing whether your habits paid off. Or you could look at your walking pace right now.

A new study followed nearly 4,000 adults in their 80s and found that the fastest walkers, people moving quicker than 93 percent of their peers, were 50 percent less likely to develop cognitive impairment, and 60 percent less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s or another dementia. Brain scans backed it up: these fast walkers had slower memory decline and better-preserved hippocampal volume, the brain region most tied to memory.

Walking briskly requires your brain, heart, lungs, and nervous system to coordinate in real time. Losing that coordination may be one of the earliest signs your brain is changing.

Luckily gait speed is trainable. Focus on cadence, not just stride. Add short bursts of brisk walking a few times a week. Strengthen your hips and core. Swing your arms.

We’ve spent years obsessing over how much we sleep. But this study suggests that when you sleep may matter just as much—and for some outcomes, perhaps even more.

Researchers followed more than 60,000 adults and found that people with the most consistent sleep schedules had substantially lower risks of all-cause, cancer, and cardiometabolic mortality than those with highly irregular schedules. Sleep regularity was actually a stronger predictor of mortality than sleep duration.

That doesn’t mean sleep duration suddenly doesn’t matter. It absolutely does. Most adults should still aim for roughly 7-9 hours of sleep per night, and there are countless studies linking both chronically short and excessively long sleep with poorer health outcomes.

It’s also important to remember that this was an observational study. People with consistent sleep schedules may also differ in many other ways—they may exercise more, eat better, have steadier jobs, lower stress, or better overall health. The researchers adjusted for many of these factors, but residual confounding is always possible.

Still, the findings make intuitive sense. Constantly shifting your sleep and wake times is, in many ways, a form of self-imposed shift work, or jet-lag. Our circadian clocks evolved to anticipate regular cycles of light, food, activity, and rest—not wildly different bedtimes every night.

So if you’re looking to improve your sleep, don’t just focus on getting enough hours. Try going to bed and waking up at roughly the same time every day. Your body—and possibly your long-term health—may thank you.

Study: Windred DP, et al. Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: A prospective cohort study. Sleep. 2024;47(1):zsad253.

Breathwork, meditation, time in nature, meaningful relationships, and real recovery all help calm an overactive stress response.

You don’t have to overhaul your life overnight. Start with one habit. Then another.

Your body is constantly responding to the signals you give it—and even small, consistent changes can help move it away from chronic inflammation and back toward health.

“Trusting the experts” is used in religion and despotic authoritarianism, it has no place in science or a free society. There was a day when science hailed cocaine as a wonder anesthetic for toothaches and pain, sold over-the-counter in tonics and lozenges for everything from depression to impotence—until addiction rates exploded (over 200,000 cases in the US by the early 1900s), leading to its ban under the 1914 Harrison Narcotic Act amid reports of hallucinations and dependency.  
  
Heroin followed a parallel path: introduced by Bayer in 1898 as a “non-addictive” alternative to morphine, it was marketed as a cough syrup safe even for children’s colds, with ads depicting spoonfuls for sore throats and claiming it was five times more effective. By the 1910s, its addictive nature became undeniable, prompting Bayer to discontinue it in 1913 and the FDA to ban it in 1924. In the mid-20th century, cigarette smoking was promoted for digestion in 1930s-50s ads, like those for Camels asserting it stimulated digestive fluids and aided alkalinity, with doctors endorsing brands as “healthier” or less irritating—until cancer links emerged in the 1940s, resulting in a 1951 FTC ban on such claims.  
  
Lobotomies, developed in 1936, severed frontal lobe connections through crude methods like ice picks inserted via the eyes, positioned as a quick “fix” for depression and mental agitation based on early neurology. Despite risks including a 15% death rate, relapses, and severe personality changes (as seen in Rosemary Kennedy’s case), it was performed widely until banned by 1967 due to ethical outcries and fatal complications. Finally, electroshock therapy was used from the 1950s-70s as a “conversion” tool for homosexuality, which mainstream medicine considered a mental disorder until the 1970s; often paired with aversion shocks during exposure to same-gender images, it affected thousands in the UK and US and wasn’t discontinued until after the 1973 diagnosis declassification.
